# Systematick

<p class="sx-lede">Everyone had investment ideas. Very few had a way to check them.</p>

Systematick is a web app where investors write their own trading rules and test them on Indian stock-market history. It uses the index as it actually was on each day, keeps the companies that later failed, and charges every trade its real costs. I founded it, and I design and build it.

<p class="sx-label">The problem</p>

## Most backtests flatter the strategy

A backtest replays a rule on past prices to see how it would have done. Most tools quietly use today's list of index companies for every past year, so the companies that collapsed or were removed simply vanish, and the results look better than they were. Others let a rule use information that was not yet known on the day it traded.

I wanted a tool that would tell an investor the uncomfortable answer as readily as the flattering one.
:::

::: {.sx-section}
<p class="sx-label">What I built</p>

## A rule language, an honest engine, and a report that shows its working

::: {.sx-two}

::: {}
Rules are written in **SAFAL**, a small language I designed so that an investing idea reads almost like a sentence: `BUY = SMA(50) CROSS_ABOVE SMA(200) AND RSI(14) < 70`. The editor checks each rule as you type. A rule is turned into a syntax tree and evaluated, never run as code, so a user cannot break or misuse the system through it.

The backtest engine runs inside the user's own browser: Python compiled to WebAssembly, in the background of the page. The server only runs the scheduled daily signals. This keeps running costs close to zero, which is why backtests are unlimited, even on the free plan.

I learned that the data is as much the product as the screen. The engine is only honest if the history underneath it is: which companies were in the index on each date, which were delisted, and how every split, bonus and merger changed what an investor held.
:::

<ol class="sx-flow" aria-label="How a backtest runs (simplified)">
<li><b>Write a rule</b><span>In SAFAL, checked as you type</span></li>
<li><b>Parse it</b><span>Into a syntax tree; never executed as code</span></li>
<li><b>Replay history in the browser</b><span>Index members as they were on each date; delisted companies kept; corporate actions applied</span></li>
<li><b>Trade realistically</b><span>Decide on each day's close, fill at the next day's open, charge Indian brokerage, taxes and fees</span></li>
<li><b>Report against the index</b><span>Returns, falls, every trade, and the assumptions behind them</span></li>
</ol>

:::

<p class="sx-label">Where it stands</p>

## A public beta, used and still being tested

Systematick is live as a public beta. Everything is free until 31 December 2026; after that there will be a free plan and a Pro plan at ₹365 a year. It has 250+ users as of October 2026. Next is a daily screener that sends a strategy's signals on Telegram the evening before each trading day.

It began as the next step after my [automated trading system](/projects/automated-trading/index-en.html), which executed other people's recommendations. Systematick starts one step earlier: how an investor defines an idea and checks it against an honest history.

<blockquote class="sx-pull">
<p>If I rebuilt it today, what would I do first?</p>
<p>Design the explanation alongside the calculation. It is easy to add another metric later; it is much harder to make an opaque result explainable after the fact.</p>
</blockquote>
:::
